text: Since Apache Kafka 4.2 (Feb 2026), share groups ('Kafka Queues', KIP-932) are production-ready. Several consumers in a share group can read the same partition with per-record acknowledgement, so the number of consumers can exceed the number of partitions.
why: Updates the partition-limits-parallelism rule for current Kafka versions.

text: AWS offers this fan-out pattern as managed services: publish once to an SNS topic and SNS pushes a copy to every subscribed SQS queue, where workers poll and process at their own pace.
why: Gives readers a concrete, managed version of the stream + broker fan-out pattern.

text: Browsers identify images from their first bytes using the WHATWG MIME Sniffing rules, which recognise ICO, BMP, GIF, WebP, PNG and JPEG signatures. SVG is not sniffed: it must be served with Content-Type image/svg+xml.
why: Explains exactly which 'header' the browser checks and the SVG exception.

text: Examples of format signatures: PNG always starts with the 8 bytes 89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A, JPEG with FF D8 FF, BMP with the ASCII letters 'BM', and GIF with 'GIF87a' or 'GIF89a'.
why: Makes 'the header tells the format' concrete.

text: A static-file handler must not let the URL path escape the static folder (e.g. /static/../../etc/passwd). Werkzeug's send_from_directory, used by Flask, applies safe_join to 'Safely join zero or more untrusted path components to a trusted base directory to avoid escaping the base directory.'
why: Path traversal is the classic bug in hand-written static or /raw handlers.

text: When your own handler returns file bytes, set the Content-Type header yourself (for S3, e.g. from the object's stored content type). MDN warns that browsers use the MIME type, not the file extension, so servers must send the correct type; nginx does this for static files by mapping extensions to MIME types.
why: A custom /raw handler loses the automatic Content-Type that static servers provide.

text: Django serves static files itself only in development (runserver with DEBUG=True); its docs say this method is 'grossly inefficient and probably insecure, so it is unsuitable for production'. In production a web server, a CDN or WhiteNoise serves them.
why: Prevents readers from serving static files through Django in production.

text: GitHub's 2021 engineering post reports that generating one image takes 280 ms on average, the service produces around two million 'unique-ish' images per day, and 40% of requests are served a cached image.
why: Real numbers show why on-demand generation plus caching beats pre-generating every repository.

text: GitHub's generator is 'a little Node.js app' that fetches data through the GitHub GraphQL API, fills an HTML template and captures it with Puppeteer. Rendering HTML in a headless browser is an alternative to drawing with an image library.
why: Shows a second, widely used way to build the prototype.

text: Pillow, the maintained fork of PIL, has its own C imaging core and links libraries such as libjpeg, zlib, libtiff and FreeType. To drive ImageMagick from Python you use a separate binding such as Wand.
why: Corrects the PIL-uses-ImageMagick claim with the right library names.

text: The CDN's TTL is usually set by the origin's Cache-Control header: s-maxage sets freshness for shared caches such as CDNs and overrides max-age there, so a card can stay a day at the CDN without browsers caching it as long.
why: Tells readers how the 'some TTL' is actually configured.

text: Open Graph requires four properties on every page: og:title, og:type, og:image and og:url. og:image is 'An image URL which should represent your object within the graph.'
why: Gives the minimal tag set needed to make a link render a snippet.
